description: Hello! We are four undergraduate students studying STEM at UC Irvine! Our team consists of a data scientist, a UX designer, and two software engineers. We love having fun while pursuing our passion for building things together. For this project, we’re creating a map application for Mars, designed to help spacefarers explore and navigate the Martian surface.
summary: We developed a layered, integrated map of Gale Crater that helps astrofarers plan and carry out safe, efficient Marswalks. Bringing data from multiple NASA missions into a single Google Maps–style view, our application includes landmarks, elevation layers, physics-based temperature + dust devil maps, and hazard warning zones. Users can plan multi-stop routes between landmarks and destinations, get warned when a route passes through or ends in a hazard zone, and keep navigating offline. Instead of referencing through separate datasets, an explorer can see the terrain, conditions, and risks along their route all in one place. The first astronauts on Mars will need the best map possible, and ours supports mission planning, research, and education. Its modular design also extends beyond Gale Crater to other regions of Mars.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Our project is a Google Maps style application for Gale Crater where astrofarers can browse through landmarks, view terrain by elevation layer, temperature heatmaps, see warning zones for hazards, and view dangerous weather. They can also plan terrain-informed routes with multiple stops or navigate to specified area of Mars, and the app warns them when a route passes through or ends in a hazard zone. Navigation works offline using downloaded map data. Our app is modular so it can easily work for other areas of Mars as well.

What benefits does it have?

The main benefit is that the app puts all of the information above into one map, so users don’t have to cross-reference orbital imagery, elevation models, thermal data and rover weather-station readings, which can be very difficult to read. Hazard filtering and proximity warnings also help astrofarers spot risks early, and offline support keeps it usable in places where connection is limited. Rovers can only measure temperature at one moving spot so our heatmap intelligently extrapolates region-wide temperatures so astrofarers have a constantly updated and accurate temperature map of anywhere on Mars. The app can be accessible for mobile devices and desktop so astrofarers and Earthlings can both learn and safely plan a route on Gale Crater. The temperature model is open source and follows Mars Physics so it can be used at any location of Mars as long as there is a present weather station nearby.

What's our intended impact?

Our goal is to make space, starting with Mars, easier to understand and move across safely, whether it be for mission planning, research, or education. Our application also gives the public a clear and interactive way to explore Mars! With the KRC thermal model dating back to 1968, and the Mars Climate Database being largely restrictive with its low resolution, our temperature model and hazard tracking provides a new and modern way to model Mars.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Figma, HTML, JavaScript, Python (NumPy, pandas, rasterio, scikit-learn), TypeScript, GDAL, QGIS

How is your project creative?

We combined several layers of information and Mars data into one interface (elevation, temperature, and hazards). There are so many different ways to present all of this information. Choosing a form that is both visually appealing and intuitive to the user definitely requires a lot of creativity. Elevation layers can be peeled back, and the heatmap switches between air and surface temperature. The temperature model uses a Physics Guided Residual Learning Model, a 1D thermal model gives a physics baseline, and a neural network model trained on Curiosity’s REMS data to correct the residual. In order for the heatmap to be kept up to date within hours we used vectorized NumPy arrays so we can process over 530,000 columns in a few hours, this way astrofarers can have accurate and fast temperature readings to ensure their survival. We present this using a temperature view also includes a seasonal estimator and supports sensor input to bring in more real-time data. Landmark labels fade when searching so the result stands out. The dust devil predictor compiles various thermal and elevation data that provides a dust devil heuristic. We found higher resolution thermal data replacing 3km TES with a 100m Themis map allowing our heat and dust devil maps to reach a 30x higher resolution.

What factors did your team consider?

We worked with and considered the limits of NASA data, especially the gaps in the weather and temperature data. We also prioritized safety, making sure warnings are visible in a timely manner. We also rigorously validated our heatmap and dust devil index by making sure our maps follow weather mechanics, and used held out sols (Martian Days) instead of random rows to prevent data leaks. Other considerations were offline mode (users may not have reliable connection), usability on smaller screens, and different users (mission planners, astronauts, and general users).
